procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Special Judge, SC/ST Act, seisin of the trial in respect of FIR No. 53 of 2000
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 06.10.2015 passed by the trial court on an application filed by the complainant Harkesh Meena under Section 319 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) summoning the appellants as additional accused persons.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants challenged the trial court's order by filing S. B. Criminal Revision Petition No.1355/2015 before the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur Bench, Jaipur. The High Court dismissed the revision petition on 11.01.2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, three in number, approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal No. 763 of 2017 after the High Court dismissed their revision petition. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of summoning the appellants under Section 319 Cr.P.C.

directions: The order of summoning the appellants under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. can be exercised to summon a person named in the FIR but not charge-sheeted, without the court being satisfied that there is much stronger evidence than a mere possibility of their complicity, especially when police investigation supported their alibi.

facts: The appellants were named in the FIR but were not included in the charge-sheet by the police.
A police investigation had collected documentary and other evidence which supported the appellants' plea of alibi, making their presence at the scene of the crime doubtful.
During the trial, the trial court summoned the appellants under Section 319 Cr.P.C.

The trial court's decision was based on the examination-in-chief of the complainant and other witnesses, which was essentially the same as their earlier statements to the police (u/s 161 Cr.P.C.) that the investigation had already found unconvincing.
law: The power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is a discretionary and extraordinary power that must be exercised sparingly and not in a casual or cavalier manner.
To summon a person under Section 319, the court must be satisfied based on strong and cogent evidence that has emerged during the trial.
The standard of satisfaction required is higher than that needed for framing a charge. It requires "stronger evidence than a mere probability of his complicity."
A court is duty-bound to consider all available material, including evidence collected during the police investigation, when forming its prima facie opinion to summon an additional accused.
application: The Supreme Court found that the trial court had acted in a "casual and cavalier manner."

The evidence recorded during the trial was nothing more than a repetition of statements already made to the police, which the investigation had found to be doubtful in light of evidence supporting the appellants' alibi.

The trial court was duty-bound to consider the investigation records that supported the alibi and to assess whether the trial evidence was "much stronger" than a mere possibility of the appellants' involvement.
The Court determined that the trial court failed to apply this higher standard of satisfaction. It ignored the contradictory evidence from the investigation and wrongly issued the summoning order.
The High Court also erred by simply agreeing with the trial court's order without independently scrutinizing the material.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the summoning order, holding that the power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. was improperly exercised. The trial court failed to apply the required high standard of satisfaction, which demands much stronger evidence than a mere possibility of complicity, especially when the police investigation had already collected significant evidence supporting the appellants' alibi.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. can be exercised to summon a person named in the FIR but not charge-sheeted, without the court being satisfied that there is much stronger evidence than a mere possibility of their complicity, especially when police investigation supported their alibi.
appellant_arguments: The trial court improperly summoned the appellants based only on witness depositions, which were essentially the same as their earlier statements to the police.
The court ignored the substantial evidence gathered during the police investigation, which found the witness statements doubtful and clinchingly showed that the appellants' alibi was correct.
To exercise power under Section 319 Cr.P.C., the court must be satisfied that there is 'much stronger evidence than a mere possibility' of complicity, a standard that was not met here.
The trial court and the High Court failed to consider the exculpatory material on record before passing the summoning order.
respondent_arguments: The trial court rightly exercised its power based on the depositions of witnesses before it, which constituted 'evidence' that the appellants may have committed the offense.
The exercise of power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. by the trial court was not unwarranted.
The High Court correctly upheld the trial court's order, finding no illegality or perversity.

cases.case_name: Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab & Ors.
cases.principle: To explain the purpose behind the provision of Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which grants power to the court to proceed against persons not named as accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power to summon an additional accused under Section 319 of the Criminal Procedure Code must not be exercised in a casual or cavalier manner.
obiter: The court is the sole repository of justice and a duty is cast upon it to uphold the rule of law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The trial court acted in a casual and cavalier manner by summoning the appellants. Although a court can exercise its power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. based on trial depositions, in this case, those depositions were merely a repetition of earlier statements recorded by the police. Given the plethora of evidence collected during the investigation that supported the appellants' alibi and cast doubt on the witnesses, the trial court was duty-bound to consider that exculpatory material. The court failed to do so and did not satisfy itself that 'much stronger evidence' of complicity had emerged, as required. The High Court compounded this error by blissfully ignoring the same material.
legal_tests_applied: When considering summoning a person under Section 319 Cr.P.C., particularly where the police investigation has found exculpatory evidence, the court must form a prima facie opinion based on whether 'much stronger evidence than mere possibility of their complicity has come on record'.
policy_considerations: The constitutional mandate under Articles 20 and 21 of the Constitution of India provides a protective umbrella for the smooth administration of justice, making adequate provisions to ensure a fair and efficacious trial so that the accused does not get prejudiced.

The court is the sole repository of justice and a duty is cast upon it to uphold the rule of law and ensure that the criminal administration of justice works properly, so that an innocent does not get punished but at the same time, the guilty are brought to book.
